hero.h1: How the soil food web works
hero.intro: Healthy soil is a living system. Billions of organisms, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, and micro-arthropods, form a web of relationships with plants that feeds them, builds the soil around them, and protects them. Here’s how it works.

elaine.line: Dr. Elaine taught that a vegetable sends about 60% of the energy it captures from sunlight below ground, and about half of that leaks from the roots as sugars, proteins and carbohydrates. She called them cakes and cookies.

source.credit: Dr. Elaine Ingham, “How to Build Great Soil, Part 1”, Diego Footer, 11:58

elaine.note: Elaine lecture copy, approve: Linnea or Evan. The 60% is attributed to Dr. Ingham by name; the nutrient cycling mechanism stays without a percentage.

mechanisms.title: The soil food web
mechanisms.body: Plants don’t feed alone. Through their roots, they release sugars and other compounds that attract and feed a community of microorganisms, and in return that community delivers nutrients, builds structure, and defends its host. This web of eating and being eaten is what makes soil function.

animation.title: The Soil Food Web
animation.note: Animation: “The Soil Food Web”, existing asset, Vimeo 372925873

quote.text: Our job is to put back the full diversity.
quote.credit: Dr. Elaine Ingham, “How to Build Great Soil, Part 1”, Diego Footer, 25:44

elaine.note: Elaine lecture copy, approve: Linnea or Evan

mechanisms.title: Nutrient cycling
mechanisms.body: A plant sends a large share of the carbon it fixes into the root zone, and much of that feeds soil microbes. Bacteria and fungi produce enzymes that break down minerals and organic matter, unlocking the nutrients they contain. When protozoa and nematodes consume those bacteria and fungi, the surplus is released right at the root, in plant-available form. The plant controls the exchange, drawing what it needs, when it needs it.
mechanisms.note: This sentence read “30 to 40% of the sugars” with no citation. That figure is Dr. Ingham's teaching number; the peer-reviewed review cited here reports lower shares for cereals than for pasture grasses, so the copy states the direction rather than a percentage. Wording to approve: Linnea or Evan.
mechanisms.source: Kuzyakov, Y. and Domanski, G. (2000). Carbon input by plants into the soil. Review. Journal of Plant Nutrition and Soil Science 163: 421 to 431.

elaine.line: Dr. Elaine described root exudates as a phone call to the pizza delivery guy: the plant orders exactly the nutrient it lacks that day, and microbes deliver.

source.credit: Dr. Elaine Ingham, “How to Build Great Soil, Part 1”, Diego Footer, 15:03

quote.text: Put the plant back in control of its own life.
quote.credit: Dr. Elaine Ingham, “How to Build Great Soil, Part 1”, Diego Footer, 16:32

elaine.note: Elaine lecture copy, approve: Linnea or Evan

mechanisms.title: Building soil structure
mechanisms.body: Beneficial bacteria produce glues that bind soil particles into microaggregates; fungal hyphae weave those into larger macroaggregates. The result behaves like a sponge: holding water for extended periods, letting air flow in, resisting erosion by wind and rain, and reducing the need for irrigation.

elaine.line: Bacteria glue particles together the way you would grab the dinner table in a flood. Fungi tie those crumbs together like string around small packages.

sources.credit: Dr. Elaine Ingham, “How to Build Great Soil, Part 1”, Diego Footer, 5:31
Dr. Elaine Ingham, “How to Build Great Soil, Part 1”, Diego Footer, 9:55

quote.text: The only thing that truly builds structure in your soil is life.
quote.credit: Dr. Elaine Ingham, “How to Build Great Soil, Part 1”, Diego Footer, 4:25

mechanisms.title: Suppressing weeds
mechanisms.body: Beneficial fungi secrete enzymes that gradually acidify their surroundings, slowing the bacteria that convert nitrogen into nitrate, the form many fast-growing weeds depend on. As the fungal community establishes, conditions shift to favor the plants you’re growing.

elaine.line: Dr. Elaine taught that a weed sends about 20% of its fixed energy to its roots, far less than the crops we grow.

source.credit: Dr. Elaine Ingham, “How to Build Great Soil, Part 1”, Diego Footer, 2:24

elaine.note: Elaine lecture copy, approve: Linnea or Evan

mechanisms.title: Protecting plants from pests and disease
mechanisms.body: Most disease-causing organisms do best where oxygen is scarce. Below ground, well-structured soil keeps the root zone oxygen-rich, favoring the beneficial organisms that compete with, inhibit, and prey on pathogens. Above ground, covering leaves and stems with beneficial microorganisms, applied as compost extracts and teas, fills the niches that pests and diseases would otherwise occupy. A surface already inhabited leaves little room for invaders.

elaine.line: Kill broadly and the fast organisms return first. Dr. Elaine compared it to gangsters moving into a trashed city block.

source.credit: Dr. Elaine Ingham, “How to Build Great Soil, Part 1”, Diego Footer, 7:32

quote.text: There is no way to kill just the bad guys.
quote.credit: Dr. Elaine Ingham, “How to Build Great Soil, Part 1”, Diego Footer, 7:06

mechanisms.title: Sequestering carbon, avoiding emissions
mechanisms.body: Plants pull carbon from the atmosphere and invest much of it into the soil, where it is built into microbial bodies, soil aggregates, and long-lived fungal networks. Biological management also avoids emissions at the source: less synthetic fertilizer to manufacture and transport, and fewer fuel-intensive passes over the field.

bridge.title: From science to practice
bridge.body: Practitioners apply this science through the Soil Food Web Approach: observe and assess the life under the microscope, incubate beneficial biology in compost, multiply and apply it with extracts and teas, and manage and monitor holistically.
